short: The set of things a Muslim holds to be true, as opposed to the things a Muslim does.
long: The root means to tie a knot, so aqidah is what the heart is tied to and does not untie. It covers Allah, His angels, His books, His messengers, the Last Day, and the decree. Fiqh answers what you do; aqidah answers what you hold true.

short: The belief that Allah is one, without partner, without equal, and alone deserving of worship.
long: The word means to make one, or to declare one. Surah al-Ikhlas states it in four short lines: He is One, the Eternal Refuge, He does not beget and was not begotten, and there is nothing comparable to Him (Qur'an 112). Tawhid is not only the claim that one God exists. It is that only He is worshipped.

short: Oneness of lordship: that Allah alone creates, owns, sustains and controls everything that exists.
long: This is the belief that there is one Creator running one universe, and the Qur'an notes that even the idolaters of Makkah admitted this much when asked who made the heavens and the earth. That is why it is not, by itself, enough to make someone a Muslim. The three part division of tawhid is a teaching framework, used widely since Ibn Taymiyyah; some scholars prefer a two part arrangement, and the difference is about how to teach it rather than what is true.

short: Oneness of worship: that prayer, vows, sacrifice, hope and fear are directed to Allah alone.
long: This is the part the messengers were sent with, and the part people have always argued over. To believe Allah made you is one thing; to bring every act of worship to Him and to no one else is another. Its exact opposite is shirk.

short: Allah's names and attributes, affirmed as He described them, without denial and without resemblance to creation.
long: The Qur'an gives Allah names and describes Him with attributes, and it also says there is nothing like Him (Qur'an 42:11). Sunni theology holds both halves at once: affirm what He said about Himself, and do not picture it as a larger version of something created. How far to explain the more difficult descriptions is exactly where the Sunni schools of creed part company.

short: The Qur'anic statement that Allah rose over the Throne, and the classic test case for reading divine attributes.
long: The Qur'an says the Most Merciful rose over the Throne (Qur'an 20:5). Atharis affirm the wording and leave the manner to Allah, quoting Imam Malik: the rising is known, the how is unknown, and asking about it is an innovation. Many Ash'aris and Maturidis read it as dominion and authority, to keep any bodily picture away. All three agree that Allah is not contained by a place.

short: Likening Allah to His creation, which the Qur'an rules out with the words: there is nothing like Him.
long: Tashbih is imagining Allah as a bigger, stronger version of something you have already seen. Its mirror error is ta'til, emptying His names and attributes of any real meaning. Sunni creed walks between the two: He is real, He is described, and He is not comparable (Qur'an 42:11).

short: Leaving the meaning of a difficult divine attribute to Allah, as opposed to interpreting it figuratively.
long: When the texts describe Allah with a hand, a face, or a rising, scholars took two broad roads. Tafwid affirms the word and consigns its reality to Allah without explaining it. Ta'wil interprets it within what the Arabic allows, such as hand meaning power. Atharis lean to the first and Ash'aris and Maturidis often to the second, and each counts the other as Sunni.

short: The belief that the people of Paradise will see their Lord with their eyes, after death.
long: The Qur'an says that on that Day some faces will be radiant, looking at their Lord (Qur'an 75:22-23), and sound hadiths compare the sight to seeing the full moon without crowding. Sunni Islam affirms this sight in the next life while denying that anyone sees Allah in this one. The Mu'tazila denied it altogether, and Twelver Shia theology also generally rejects a literal vision.

short: Giving to something other than Allah what belongs to Allah alone, above all worship.
long: The word means to make a partner or to share. The Qur'an says Allah does not forgive that a partner be set up with Him, and forgives what is less than that for whom He wills (Qur'an 4:48). Commentators read that of the one who dies without repenting, since the Qur'an elsewhere promises forgiveness to whoever turns back. Scholars distinguish major shirk, which takes a person outside Islam, from minor shirk, which is a grave sin but does not.

short: Minor shirk: acts like showing off in worship, which damage sincerity without putting a person outside Islam.
long: The Prophet peace be upon him called showing off the lesser shirk, in a report collected by Imam Ahmad. Swearing by other than Allah, and saying what Allah and so and so willed, belong to the same family. The point is not to make a believer anxious about every sentence, but to keep worship pointed in one direction.

short: Disbelief: rejecting or refusing what a person knows Allah has revealed.
long: The root means to cover, the way a farmer covers a seed with soil, so kufr is covering a truth that has already reached you. Scholars separate major kufr, which places someone outside Islam, from the lesser kufr that some texts use for serious sins committed by a believer. Deciding that a particular person is a disbeliever is a scholarly and judicial matter, not a conversational one.

short: Hypocrisy: showing belief outwardly while concealing disbelief, or acting against the faith one claims.
long: The Qur'an gives the munafiqun a surah of their own and says the hypocrites will be in the lowest depth of the Fire (Qur'an 4:145). Scholars distinguish nifaq of belief, which is disbelief in disguise, from nifaq of conduct: the well known signs of lying, breaking a promise, and betraying a trust, reported in Bukhari and Muslim. The second kind was taught as a mirror for the believer to check himself, not as a label to hand to others.

short: Declaring a specific Muslim to be a disbeliever, a ruling classical scholars fenced with heavy conditions.
long: Scholarship treats takfir as a judgement with conditions and impediments: ignorance, misreading, compulsion, and the absence of clear proof all block it. The Prophet peace be upon him warned that when a man calls his brother a disbeliever it returns to one of the two, in a report in Bukhari and Muslim. Saying that a statement is disbelief is not the same as saying the person who said it is a disbeliever, and the second was left to qualified scholars.

short: Faith: belief in Allah, His angels, His books, His messengers, the Last Day, and the decree.
long: The six articles come from the hadith of Jibril in Sahih Muslim, where the angel asks the Prophet peace be upon him what faith is and then confirms his answer. Iman is more than agreement in the mind; the texts tie it to the tongue and to the limbs as well. Most Sunni scholars hold that iman increases and decreases, while the Hanafi and Maturidi tradition holds that its essence stays fixed even as its light grows.

short: Submission to Allah: outwardly the five pillars, inwardly the handing over of the whole self.
long: The word comes from a root carrying both surrender and peace, and the Qur'an calls it the religion with Allah (Qur'an 3:19). In the hadith of Jibril, islam is answered with the five pillars, iman with the six articles of belief, and ihsan with the quality of worship. So islam is the outward frame, iman the inner conviction, and ihsan the finish on both.

short: To worship Allah as though you see Him, and if you do not see Him, knowing that He sees you.
long: The definition is the Prophet's own wording in the hadith of Jibril, collected in Bukhari and Muslim. The word means to do a thing beautifully, and it reaches past worship into how a person treats people and animals. It is the difference between a prayer performed and a prayer attended.

short: The six articles of faith: Allah, His angels, His books, His messengers, the Last Day, and the decree.
long: They are listed together in the hadith of Jibril, recorded in Sahih Muslim, when the Prophet peace be upon him is asked what faith is. The Qur'an gathers most of them in a single verse about the believers (Qur'an 2:285). These six are the frame, and almost every other question of creed is a detail hanging inside one of them.

short: The natural disposition every person is born with, leaning toward recognising one Creator.
long: The Qur'an speaks of the fitrah of Allah upon which He made people (Qur'an 30:30), and the Prophet peace be upon him said that every child is born upon the fitrah, in Bukhari and Muslim. It is not a memory of doctrine but a leaning, and it is easily covered over by habit and upbringing. In fiqh the same word names the acts of natural cleanliness, which is a separate meaning of one root.

short: Allah's decree: that He knows, wrote, willed and created all that happens, without forcing anyone to sin.
long: Scholars describe four levels to it: Allah's knowledge of everything, its writing in the Preserved Tablet, His will, and His creating it. The Qur'an says He created every thing in due measure (Qur'an 54:49), and the word itself carries measure rather than blind fate. Belief in qadr is the sixth article of faith in the hadith of Jibril. It does not remove your choice and it is not a reason to stop trying, which is why the Prophet peace be upon him answered a question about it by telling the man to act.

short: Allah's decree carried out: the partner word to qadr, though scholars differ over which term means which.
long: One common explanation is that qadr is the eternal measuring and qada is the putting into effect, while other scholars reverse the two. Either way, when the pair is used together they mean one thing: nothing reaches you from outside Allah's knowledge and will. In fiqh the same word means making up a missed prayer or fast, and it also means a judge's ruling, which are different uses of one root.

short: Human choice: real enough to be answerable for, and never outside Allah's knowledge and creation.
long: Two old errors sit on either side of the road. The Jabriyyah said a person is compelled, like a feather in wind; the Qadariyyah said a person creates his own acts independently of Allah's decree. Ahl al-Sunnah hold both truths together: Allah creates the act, and the servant genuinely chooses and earns it, a position the Ash'aris call kasb.

short: The appointed term of a life or a nation, which does not arrive early or run late.
long: The Qur'an says that when their term comes they cannot delay it by an hour, nor bring it forward (Qur'an 7:34). It is why a believer can take medicine and take cover without any contradiction: means are commanded, outcomes are decreed. The reports that keeping ties of kinship lengthens a life are explained as blessing placed in the time given, or as what stands in the angels' record rather than in Allah's knowledge.

short: Everything real that lies beyond the reach of the senses, known only because Allah reported it.
long: The Qur'an opens by describing the God fearing as those who believe in the unseen (Qur'an 2:3). It covers Allah Himself, the angels, the jinn, the grave, the Day of Judgement, Paradise and the Fire. Scholars call these matters sam'iyyat, things received by report, because reason can accept them but could never have discovered them. Claiming private access to the unseen, through stars or cards or spirits, is claiming something the Qur'an reserves to Allah.

short: Revelation: Allah's speech conveyed to a prophet, directly, from behind a veil, or through an angel.
long: The Qur'an describes exactly those three modes (Qur'an 42:51), and says the Prophet peace be upon him did not speak from desire, but that it was revelation revealed (Qur'an 53:3-4). Revelation of this kind came to prophets only, and it ended with the death of the last of them. Nothing after him, however sincere or however true it feels, carries the same authority. Where the Qur'an uses the same verb of the bee or of the mother of Musa, scholars read inspiration rather than prophecy.

short: Inspiration placed in a heart, which may be true but is not revelation and is not proof for anyone else.
long: The Qur'an uses the word for the soul being inspired with its wrong and its right (Qur'an 91:8). Sunni scholars accept that a righteous person may be given true insight, and still refuse to build a ruling on it, because ilham is not protected from error. If an inspiration contradicts the Qur'an or the Sunnah it is set aside without argument. Sufi writing uses kashf, unveiling, for a similar idea, under the same rule.

short: Prophethood: Allah choosing certain men to receive revelation and deliver it, ending with Muhammad, peace be upon him.
long: The Qur'an names many prophets and says every nation was sent a warner. A rasul is usually described as one sent with a new law or to a rejecting people, and a nabi as one continuing a law already given, though scholars word the distinction in different ways. Prophets are protected in conveying the message, a quality called ismah. Muhammad peace be upon him is the seal of them, so no prophet comes after him (Qur'an 33:40).

short: The scriptures Allah revealed, belief in them being one of the six articles of faith.
long: A Muslim believes that Allah spoke to earlier communities and that those revelations were true when they were given (Qur'an 2:285). The Qur'an names the Tawrat given to Musa, the Zabur to Dawud, the Injil to Isa, and pages given to Ibrahim and Musa. The mainstream position is that earlier scriptures were altered in wording or in handling over time, so present copies are not taken as authority, while the Qur'an is held to be the final one and preserved.

short: A miracle given to a prophet as proof of prophethood, which his opponents are unable to match.
long: The word means that which renders others powerless. The staff of Musa, the healing given to Isa, and the splitting of the moon are examples, and the standing miracle of Muhammad peace be upon him is the Qur'an itself. A mu'jizah is public, tied to a claim of prophethood, and impossible to imitate, and that is what separates it from a karamah.

short: An extraordinary event granted to a righteous believer, with no claim to prophethood attached.
long: Ahl al-Sunnah affirm karamat, pointing to Maryam finding provision out of season (Qur'an 3:37) and to the sleepers of the cave. The Mu'tazila denied them. Sunni scholars then set one plain rule: a person's uprightness on the Sunnah is the proof, not the wonder, so someone who breaks the sacred law while performing marvels is not a friend of Allah but a warning.

short: Being drawn in slowly by blessings while sinning, so that ease becomes a punishment rather than approval.
long: The Qur'an says of those who deny its signs: We will lead them on by degrees from where they do not know (Qur'an 7:182). It is the answer to a question people ask honestly, which is why the wrongdoer prospers. Comfort is not a verdict, and neither is hardship.

short: The spirit that gives a body life, whose reality Allah kept to Himself.
long: When the Prophet peace be upon him was asked about the ruh, the answer came: say, the spirit is from the affair of my Lord, and you have been given only a little knowledge (Qur'an 17:85). It is taken at death, held in the barzakh, and returned to the body at the resurrection. Many scholars use ruh and nafs for the same thing seen from two angles, while others treat them as distinct.

short: The self: the inner person that can command wrong, blame itself, or come to rest.
long: The Qur'an describes it in three states: the soul that commands evil (Qur'an 12:53), the self reproaching soul (Qur'an 75:2), and the soul at peace, called back to its Lord well pleased (Qur'an 89:27-28). These are not three souls but one self in three conditions, and a person moves between them in a single day. Struggling with the nafs is ordinary religious life, not a sign that something has gone wrong.

short: Angels: beings created from light who never disobey Allah and carry out exactly what they are commanded.
long: Belief in them is one of the six articles of faith. Their creation from light is reported in Sahih Muslim rather than in the Qur'an. They are not male or female in the human sense, they do not eat or tire, and the Qur'an says they do not disobey Allah in what He commands them and do what they are told (Qur'an 66:6). A few are named in the texts, most are not, and their number is known to Allah alone.

short: The two honourable scribes who record what every person says and does.
long: The Qur'an says over you are keepers, noble writers, who know what you do (Qur'an 82:10-12), and that not a word is uttered without a watcher ready beside him (Qur'an 50:18). The names Raqib and Atid come from reading two words of that verse as names rather than as descriptions. What they write becomes the record handed to each person on the Day of Judgement, a book that leaves out nothing small or large (Qur'an 18:49). The verses were given to produce attention rather than dread.

short: The two angels who question a person in the grave about their Lord, their religion, and their prophet.
long: They are named in a hadith reported by al-Tirmidhi, and the three questions appear in several sound narrations. The believer answers with certainty and the grave is widened for him; the one who lived heedless can only say that he heard people saying something and repeated it. This is the trial of the grave that the Prophet peace be upon him taught his companions to seek refuge from in every prayer.

short: The angel of death, who takes each soul at its appointed time by Allah's command.
long: The Qur'an says: the angel of death, who has been put in charge of you, will take you, then to your Lord you will be returned (Qur'an 32:11). The name Izra'il is widely used but does not come from the Qur'an or from an authentic hadith, where he is simply called the angel of death. Narrations describe helpers who assist him in taking souls.

short: A created race made from fire, unseen to us, who like people believe or disbelieve and are accountable.
long: The Qur'an gives them a surah of their own (Qur'an 72), reports a group of them listening to the recitation and accepting it, and says they were created from a smokeless flame of fire (Qur'an 55:15). They eat, they marry, they die, and they will be judged. They are not the spirits of dead humans, and they are not behind most of what gets blamed on them.

short: The jinn who refused to prostrate to Adam out of pride, and was expelled and granted respite.
long: The Qur'an tells the scene several times and states plainly that he was of the jinn, and so he departed from the command of his Lord (Qur'an 18:50). He asked for time until the Day they are raised and was given it. Iblis is his name, while shaytan describes what he became, and what his followers among jinn and men are called.

short: A devil: any rebellious jinn, and with the definite article, Iblis himself.
long: The Qur'an says he is an enemy to you, so take him as an enemy (Qur'an 35:6), and gives him only two tools, whispering and inviting. He cannot compel anyone; on the Day of Judgement he tells his own followers that he had no authority over them except that he called and they answered (Qur'an 14:22). The Qur'an also calls some human beings shayatin, so the word is not limited to jinn.

short: The jinn companion assigned to each person, whose work is whispering toward wrong.
long: The Prophet peace be upon him said that every one of you has a companion from the jinn and a companion from the angels, in a report in Sahih Muslim, and said that his own had submitted so that it only urged him toward good. The Qur'an uses the same word for a companion who speaks up on the Day of Judgement (Qur'an 50:23-27). It is not a double of you, a shadow self, or a source of information about your life, and most of the popular material about it goes far beyond anything the texts say.

short: The state between death and the resurrection, where the soul waits after the body is buried.
long: The word means a barrier or partition. The Qur'an uses it of the one who begs to be returned to life and is refused: behind them is a barrier until the Day they are raised (Qur'an 23:100). It is a real condition, with ease or with distress, and its details are not measurable by anything we can observe from this side.

short: The punishment or ease a person meets in the grave, before the Day of Judgement arrives.
long: The Qur'an describes the people of Fir'awn exposed to the Fire morning and evening before the Hour comes (Qur'an 40:46), and many sound hadiths describe the grave as either a garden of Paradise or a pit of the Fire. Ahl al-Sunnah affirm it as real without claiming to know how it works upon a body that has decayed or was never buried. The Mu'tazila denied it; the Sunni schools do not.

short: The Day of Resurrection, when this creation ends, the dead are raised, and everyone is judged.
long: The word means the standing, because people stand before their Lord. Its timing is known to Allah alone, though the Prophet peace be upon him described signs that come before it. The Qur'an returns to this Day constantly, not to frighten, but because a life that ends in an account is lived differently from one that does not.

short: The signs that come before the Day of Judgement, sorted by scholars into minor and major.
long: The Qur'an says its signs have already come (Qur'an 47:18), which commentators read as the sending of the final Prophet. The minor signs are gradual changes in society described across the hadith literature; the major ones are the ten listed in a report in Sahih Muslim, among them the Dajjal, the descent of Isa, Ya'juj and Ma'juj, the beast, the smoke, the sun rising from the west, and a fire that drives people to their final gathering. Reading current events as the fulfilment of signs is an old habit, and every attempt to put a date on it has been wrong so far.

short: The false messiah who appears near the end of time, claiming godhood and testing people with power.
long: He is not named in the Qur'an, but the reports about him are so numerous that Sunni scholars treat them as certain. He is described as one eyed, with disbelief written between his eyes, given power to show wonders and to control provision, and finally killed by Isa. The Prophet peace be upon him said that every prophet warned his people about him, and taught the opening verses of Surah al-Kahf as protection.

short: A rightly guided leader expected near the end of time, understood very differently by Sunni and Shia Islam.
long: In Sunni Islam he is a future man from the family of the Prophet peace be upon him who will rule with justice, described in reports collected by Abu Dawud, al-Tirmidhi and others; most scholars accepted them, while a minority, including Ibn Khaldun, criticised their chains. He is not named in the Qur'an. Twelver Shia belief is different in kind: the Mahdi there is the twelfth Imam, already born, alive in occultation, and awaited. Claimants have appeared in almost every century, and each one so far has been mistaken.

short: The descent of Isa near the end of time, to break the cross, kill the Dajjal, and rule with justice.
long: The Qur'an says he was not killed and not crucified, but that Allah raised him (Qur'an 4:157-158), and calls him a sign of the Hour (Qur'an 43:61). The hadiths describe his descent, his prayer behind the leader of the Muslims, and his death and burial afterwards like any other human being. He returns as a follower of the final Prophet, not with a new religion.

short: Two peoples held back behind a barrier built by Dhu al-Qarnayn, released as a major sign of the Hour.
long: The Qur'an tells the story of the barrier of iron and molten copper (Qur'an 18:94-98) and says that when they are released they will swarm down from every height (Qur'an 21:96). Scholars have guessed for centuries about who and where they are; the honest answer is that the texts describe a time, not a place on a map. Their release is one of the ten major signs.

short: The horn that is blown to end this world, and blown again to raise the dead.
long: The Qur'an says the horn is blown and everyone in the heavens and the earth falls dead except whom Allah wills, then it is blown a second time and they are standing, looking on (Qur'an 39:68). The angel entrusted with it is named Israfil in the hadith literature. Reports describe him holding it to his mouth, head inclined, waiting for the command.

short: The resurrection: bodies raised and souls returned, so that everyone stands for judgement.
long: The Qur'an answers the objection directly, asking who will give life to bones after they have crumbled, and replying that He who produced them the first time will (Qur'an 36:78-79). The gathering that follows is called the hashr, on an open plain where nobody is missed or overlooked. Sunni belief is that the raising is bodily and not only spiritual.

short: The reckoning: each person shown their record and questioned about the life they were given.
long: The Qur'an describes books handed to the right hand and to the left, and an easy reckoning for some (Qur'an 84:7-9). The Prophet peace be upon him said that a servant's feet will not move on that Day until he is asked about his life, his knowledge, his wealth and his body, in a report collected by al-Tirmidhi. Sound narrations also describe a group entering Paradise with no reckoning at all.

short: The record of a person's deeds, handed to them on the Day of Judgement.
long: The Qur'an says every person's record is fastened to them and will be brought out as a book found spread open, with the words: read your record, today you are sufficient as a reckoner against yourself (Qur'an 17:13-14). Elsewhere the wrongdoers say of it: what kind of book is this, it leaves out nothing small or large (Qur'an 18:49). Receiving it in the right hand is the sign of success.

short: The scale on which deeds are weighed on the Day of Judgement, with exact justice.
long: The Qur'an says the scales of justice will be set up for the Day of Resurrection, so that no soul is wronged in anything, even the weight of a mustard seed (Qur'an 21:47). Sunni belief takes this as a real scale and not only a figure of speech. Some small deeds are described as heavy upon it, far out of proportion to the effort they cost, which is worth remembering.

short: The bridge laid over Hell that everyone must cross, at speeds matching their deeds.
long: It is described in the long hadith of intercession in Bukhari and Muslim: people pass over it like lightning, like the wind, like a running horse, or crawling, and some are seized along the way. The Qur'an speaks of every one of you coming to it (Qur'an 19:71), which many commentators read as this crossing. The same word in Surah al-Fatihah means the straight path in this life, a different sense of one root.

short: The Prophet's pool, where his community drinks before entering Paradise and never thirsts again.
long: The narrations about it are numerous and agreed upon: its water whiter than milk, sweeter than honey, its cups like the stars of the sky. The Prophet peace be upon him said he will be at it ahead of his community, and that some who belonged to him will be turned away for what they introduced after him. Al-Kawthar, the river given to him in Paradise (Qur'an 108:1), is described in the reports as feeding it.

short: Intercession: one person asking Allah on behalf of another, and only by Allah's permission.
long: The Qur'an denies intercession that works like influence over a king, and affirms it with permission: who is there that can intercede with Him except by His leave (Qur'an 2:255). The greatest instance is the Maqam Mahmud, the praised station, where the Prophet peace be upon him asks for the standing to be relieved and the judgement to begin. Angels, prophets, martyrs and even a person's own children are described as interceding. Asking Allah to grant you the Prophet's intercession is agreed upon; addressing the deceased directly is where positions divide.

short: Paradise: the garden of lasting delight prepared for the believers, where nothing is lost or spoiled.
long: The word means a garden covered over by its own foliage, and the Qur'an describes rivers, shade and gardens, then says the pleasure of Allah is greater than all of it (Qur'an 9:72). A sacred hadith describes what is in it as what no eye has seen, no ear has heard, and no heart has imagined. Firdaws is named as its highest part, beneath the Throne. In Sunni belief its greatest gift is the sight of Allah Himself.

short: The Fire: the punishment prepared for those who refused, described in the Qur'an in plain and heavy terms.
long: The Qur'an gives it names and levels and says the Fire was prepared for those who reject faith (Qur'an 2:24). Sunni belief holds that believers who enter it for their sins do not remain in it, and are brought out by mercy and intercession, while disbelief carried to the grave meets a lasting punishment. The verses are not decoration, and they are also not an invitation to guess who is going there.

short: The hereafter: everything after death, from the grave to the final settling in Paradise or the Fire.
long: The Qur'an pairs it constantly with the dunya, the near life, and says the hereafter is better and more lasting (Qur'an 87:17). Belief in it is one of the six articles of faith. It is not an escape from this world; the same Qur'an teaches the believer to ask for good in both.

short: The Prophet's way in belief, worship and conduct, and the measure against which innovation is judged.
long: The word means a trodden path. In hadith study it covers what the Prophet peace be upon him said, did, and quietly approved; in fiqh it also names a recommended act; in creed it means the received way of the first generations, which is why the phrase Ahl al-Sunnah exists. Set against bid'ah, sunnah means the shape of the religion as it was handed over, rather than anyone's personal preference.

short: Innovation in religion: introducing an act of worship that has no basis in what was revealed.
long: The Prophet peace be upon him said that whoever introduces into this affair of ours something that is not from it will have it rejected, in Bukhari and Muslim. Everyone agrees that new things in worldly life are not the subject; nobody calls a printing press or a microphone bid'ah. Scholars differ on the categories: many, following al-Shafi'i and al-Izz ibn Abd al-Salam, sort innovations into praiseworthy and blameworthy, while others hold that whatever is correctly called bid'ah in religion is blameworthy, and the good cases were never bid'ah to begin with.

short: The main body of Muslims who follow the Prophet's way and the practice of his companions.
long: The name joins two things: the sunnah, and the jama'ah, the community that held to it. In creed the Sunni world recognises three schools, Ash'ari, Maturidi and Athari; in law it recognises four, Hanafi, Maliki, Shafi'i and Hanbali. Difference inside those boundaries is old and normal, and is not the same thing as stepping outside them.

short: A Sunni school of creed founded by Abu al-Hasan al-Ash'ari, defending orthodox belief with reasoned argument.
long: Al-Ash'ari trained among the Mu'tazila and then left them, turning their own methods toward defending the positions of the people of hadith. The school became associated with Shafi'i and Maliki scholarship, and with figures such as al-Ghazali, al-Razi and al-Nawawi. On the difficult attribute verses it tends toward interpretation or consignment rather than literal wording. It is one of the three creed schools recognised within Ahl al-Sunnah.

short: A Sunni school of creed founded by Abu Mansur al-Maturidi, closely tied to the Hanafi tradition.
long: It grew in Samarqand and became the creed of most Hanafis, and so of much of Turkey, Central Asia, and the Indian subcontinent. It stands close to the Ash'ari school and differs on a set of fine points, such as how far reason alone can establish that Allah must be known before revelation arrives, and whether iman itself increases and decreases. Each school counts the other as Sunni.

short: The Sunni creed school that keeps to the wording of the texts and avoids theological speculation.
long: Athar means a narration, and the approach is to affirm what the Qur'an and Sunnah say about Allah in their own words, without figurative interpretation and without asking how. It is associated with Ahmad ibn Hanbal, and later with Ibn Taymiyyah and with much modern Salafi thought. Along with the Ash'aris and Maturidis it is one of the three recognised Sunni creed schools, and the argument between the three is old, sharp, and internal.

short: Approaching Allah through a means, such as His names, your own good deeds, or a living person's du'a.
long: All schools agree on three forms: by Allah's names and attributes, by your own righteous deeds, and by asking a living righteous person to pray for you, the last shown in the hadith of the blind man and in Umar asking al-Abbas to pray for rain. They differ over tawassul by the person or rank of a prophet or saint, especially after death. Many Hanafi, Maliki, Shafi'i and Sufi scholars permit it as a form of asking Allah, while Hanbali and Salafi scholarship generally rejects it as a door to worse. All sides agree that asking the dead to grant something themselves is not tawassul at all but shirk.

short: A means of nearness to Allah, and also the name of a specific high station in Paradise.
long: The Qur'an commands: seek the means of nearness to Him (Qur'an 5:35), which the commentators explain as obedience and whatever brings a servant close. The word is also the name of a rank in Paradise which the Prophet peace be upon him said belongs to one servant only, and which he taught his community to ask for on his behalf after the call to prayer. The two meanings share a root and are often mixed up in argument.

short: Calling for help, and the disputed question of whom a Muslim may call on when it is not Allah.
long: Everyone agrees that asking a present living person for help within their ability is ordinary and permitted, and that asking anyone at all for what only Allah can give is shirk. The dispute is narrower than it sounds: calling on an absent or deceased prophet or righteous person. Many Sufi and traditional scholars read it as a request for that person's prayer and permit it, while Hanbali and Salafi scholarship reads it as calling upon the dead and forbids it. Both sides are arguing over the meaning of one line said seventeen times a day: You alone we worship, You alone we ask for help (Qur'an 1:5).

short: The Throne of Allah, the greatest created thing, above the heavens and carried by angels.
long: The Qur'an says His Throne was upon the water before the heavens and the earth were made (Qur'an 11:7), and describes angels carrying it and surrounding it with praise (Qur'an 40:7). Sunni scholars affirm it as a real created thing and warn against imagining that Allah needs it or is contained by it. The Prophet peace be upon him said that al-Firdaws, the highest part of Paradise, lies directly beneath it.

short: Something vast that extends over the heavens and the earth, which most scholars hold is distinct from the Throne.
long: The Qur'an says His Kursi extends over the heavens and the earth, and preserving them does not tire Him (Qur'an 2:255). Ibn Abbas is reported to have explained it as the place of the two feet, while others read it as His knowledge or His dominion. A narration compares the seven heavens beside the Kursi to a ring thrown into open desert, and the Kursi beside the Throne in the same way.

short: The Preserved Tablet, in which everything decreed was written down before it happened.
long: The Qur'an closes Surah al-Buruj by calling it a glorious Qur'an in a Preserved Tablet (Qur'an 85:21-22), and speaks elsewhere of the Mother of the Book (Qur'an 43:4). It is the writing stage of the decree: what is in it does not change, and what a person can still change is himself. Its reality belongs to the unseen, so speculation about its material or its size is empty.

short: The Pen, commanded to write the decree of everything that would happen until the Day of Judgement.
long: Allah swears by the pen and by what they write (Qur'an 68:1). A hadith in the collections of Abu Dawud and al-Tirmidhi reports that the first thing Allah created was the Pen, and He said to it write, and it wrote what would be until the Hour. The image is not ink and paper but a matter already settled, which is why the Prophet peace be upon him told Ibn Abbas that the pens have been lifted and the pages have dried.

also: Lote tree of the utmost boundary
short: The Lote Tree at the furthest limit, reached by the Prophet on the Night Journey.
long: The Qur'an says he saw him at a second descent, by the Lote Tree of the utmost boundary, near which is the Garden of Refuge (Qur'an 53:13-15). Scholars describe it as the boundary past which the knowledge of creation does not go, so it marks a limit rather than a location. It appears in the accounts of the Night Journey, at the stage where the five daily prayers were given.

also: Those who never heard the message
What about people who never heard of Islam
short: People who lived without a prophet's message reaching them, and the question of how they are judged.
long: The Qur'an says We do not punish until We have sent a messenger (Qur'an 17:15), which every school takes as the starting point. The Ash'ari position is that such a person is not punished, because obligation begins when the message arrives, while Maturidis hold that reason alone still obliges a person to recognise the Creator. A well known group of hadiths describes them being tested on the Day of Judgement itself, and many scholars, including within the Hanbali tradition, hold that view. What all sides agree on is that these are cases for Allah to judge, and not a category for living people to sort each other into.
